title: Partitive articles, fruits, vegetables and groceries
goal: By the end of this lesson you can talk about food and groceries using du, de la, de l' and des, switch to de after negatives and quantities, and shop with Quebec grocery vocabulary.

learn.h: Some: du, de la, de l', des
body: French needs an article where English often has 'some' or nothing at all: *Je mange du pain.* = I eat (some) bread. This is the partitive article.
Use it for an unspecified amount of something you can't count (bread, milk, water) and *des* for an unspecified number of things you can count (apples, carrots).

head: Before
Partitive
Example
rows: du pain, du fromage, du lait
de la viande, de la salade

learn.tip: If you could say 'some' in English, French needs du / de la / des.

learn.h: Like vs eat: le or du?
body: After verbs of taste (*aimer, adorer, détester, préférer*), use the definite article because you mean the thing in general: *J'aime le fromage.* (I like cheese.)
After verbs of consuming or buying (*manger, boire, acheter, prendre, vouloir*), use the partitive: *J'achète du fromage.* (I'm buying some cheese.)
After a negative, *du, de la, de l'* and *des* all become *de* (or *d'* before a vowel): *Je ne mange pas de viande.* *Il n'y a plus d'eau.*
After a quantity, also use *de* alone: *beaucoup de fruits*, *un peu de sucre*, *un kilo de pommes*, *une bouteille d'eau*, *une douzaine d'œufs*, *assez de lait*.
Exception: *être* in the negative keeps the article: *Ce n'est pas du sucre, c'est du sel.*

learn.h: Quebec: where and what you buy
body: In Quebec, *l'épicerie* is the grocery store (the supermarket), and *faire l'épicerie* means 'to do the groceries'. *Le dépanneur* is the small corner store for milk, bread and snacks.

*Une liqueur* in Quebec is a soft drink (pop), not an alcoholic liqueur as in France. Also Quebec: *des patates* (potatoes), *du blé d'Inde* (corn), *de la crème glacée* (ice cream), *un casseau* (small basket of berries).

quebec.intro: Food shopping is full of Quebec words: you 'faire l'épicerie', grab milk at the dépanneur, and order a 'liqueur' when you want pop. Some words differ from France, so it's worth knowing both.

items.note: in France, une liqueur is a sweet alcoholic drink
patates is universal in Quebec speech
épluchette de blé d'Inde = corn-husking party
in Quebec, la glace is just ice

drills.why: After a negative, the partitive becomes de.
After adorer (taste), use the definite article: le chocolat.
Liqueur = pop / soft drink in Quebec.

pron.tip: du [dü] has the tight French u; de [duh] is relaxed.
Liaison: day-ZUH; the f and s of œufs are silent in the plural.
In the singular, the f is pronounced: uh-NUF.

dialogue.en: No problem. I'll also take two soft drinks and some chips.

speak.prompt: Say what you usually eat for breakfast, using du, de la or des.
speak.model: Le matin, je mange du pain avec du fromage et je bois du café.

speak.prompt: Say two foods you don't eat or drink.
speak.model: Je ne mange pas de viande et je ne bois pas de liqueur.

speak.prompt: Ask for three things at the dépanneur, with a quantity for each.
speak.model: Je voudrais une bouteille de lait, un sac de chips et une douzaine d'œufs, s'il vous plaît.

write.prompt: Write your grocery list for the week as 5–6 sentences: what you buy, how much, and one thing you never buy.
write.model: Samedi, je fais l'épicerie. J'achète du pain, du lait et des œufs. Je prends aussi un kilo de pommes et un casseau de fraises. Pour le souper, j'achète des patates et du poulet. Je n'achète jamais de liqueur.

quiz.why: After pas, de → d' before a vowel.
Taste verbs take le / la / les.

options: to work at the corner store
quiz.why: Faire l'épicerie = to do the grocery shopping.

quiz.q: 'Ce n'est pas ___ sucre, c'est du sel.'
quiz.why: With être, the article stays after the negative.

quiz.q: Quebec 'crème glacée' in France is usually…
quiz.why: France says une glace; Quebec says crème glacée.
Quantity + de, elided before a vowel: d'œufs.
